Starting from the formal derivation of Smith & Sprinks (1975), we derived a time-dependent mild-slope equation and, from it, a higher-order dispersion relation for waves over an uneven bottom.

Using only the linear dispersion relation for steady waves, we recovered equation (2.12) of Chamberlain & Porter (1995), known as the Modified Mild-Slope Equation (MMSE). The leading-order solution shows that the modified curvature terms of the MMSE have significant effects, while the slope square terms stay negligible, consistent with the mild-slope assumption. We therefore kept all the modified curvature terms that the MSE neglects, which produced a uniform model.

We then built a numerical model with the finite element method (FEM) to predict wave scattering by a varying bottom. In general, the uniform model can predict the main features of waves over different sea beds, including sinusoidal beds and man-made bars. For sinusoidal beds, the uniform model agrees more closely with experimental data than other established models. For man-made bars, both the MMSE and the uniform model agree more closely with experimental data than the results of Kirby (1986).

A key result of the FEM model is its application to wave transformation over arbitrarily-varying bathymetry.

We are writing to share some information you may find useful about how hearing develops early in life. Children typically acquire spoken language in their first few years. If hearing is impaired during that time, a child may struggle both to speak and to understand what others say.

Often, a severely hearing-impaired (deaf) child's deficit only becomes obvious later, once communication problems have already strained family life and slowed social development. A child raised in a Deaf community that uses sign language rather than speech faces fewer of these difficulties (see our article on Deaf Culture).

For this reason, many developed countries screen newborns for hearing loss, so a deaf child is not accidentally isolated in a hearing family. Sign language is a complete way to communicate, but learning to read still depends on understanding speech, since most written languages represent word sounds with symbols.

Someone who heard well enough to learn speech and reading will keep that reading ability even if hearing later deteriorates to the point of not hearing voices. A person who never heard well enough to learn to speak, however, rarely reads with proficiency (see [4]). The evidence points the same way: the sooner hearing impairment is identified, the better a child with very insensitive hearing can learn spoken language. Listening matters for picking up a second language too.

We hope this gives you a clearer picture of why early intervention matters. If you have questions, please get in touch.

Warm regards,

Transduction is how physical and chemical signals become neural impulses. In the nervous system, it is the basic process of translating stimuli into electrical signals. In sensory transduction, specialized sensory receptors take physical or chemical inputs and turn them into electrical impulses that travel to the brain.

Look at the visual system. In the retina, rod and cone cells connect the physical world to neural communication. Light strikes these photoreceptors and changes the shape of the protein rhodopsin. That molecular shift sets off a cascade of events that alters the electrochemical gradient of the photoreceptor. As the gradient drops, so do the electrical signals sent to the brain. More light hitting the photoreceptor means fewer electrical impulses. Your brain reads that pattern and decodes the visual world with precision.

Subject: Tips for Hitchhiking in the Ruhr Area, Germany

Dear Customer,

The Ruhr Area (German: Ruhrgebiet), often just called the Ruhr, is an urban region in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. It grew out of old industrial cities: Duisburg, Oberhausen, Bottrop, Mülheim an der Ruhr, Essen, Gelsenkirchen, Bochum, Herne, Hamm, Hagen, Dortmund, Recklinghausen, Unna, and Witten.

About five million people live here. That makes the region considerably larger than Berlin, Hamburg, or Munich. Motorways crisscross the area, yet hitchhiking is harder than you'd expect, because the minor roads form a confusing tangle. The main motorways are the A1, A2, and A3.

If you hitch here, stick to those three. The smaller roads will defeat you; almost no transit traffic passes them. Germany is generally a pleasant country to hitch through, but the Ruhr is its worst stretch by far. Hitching inside the Ruhr feels like hitching in a city the size of Istanbul. Each city is independent, yet to you they will all blur into districts of one massive city.

We hope this helps you plan a safe and enjoyable trip.

Best regards,

Mobile Gaming: The Next Evolution of Co-Creation

Mobile internet is expanding what storytelling can do through electronic games that run on portable, location-aware interfaces. This is the latest step in a decades-long evolution of electronic games that aim to make the player a co-author alongside the original designers, going beyond the role of an avatar in a gameworld.

Location-aware interfaces let players pull places from the physical world into their gameworld, and the reverse, something no earlier interactive media could do. Beyond giving players a role in worldmaking, mobile games drop linear narratives in favor of cooperative storytelling built on the player's experience of place.

The "author-player" worldmaking idea is not new. Mobile games, however, push the process past the limits of traditional video games. By extending worldmaking beyond the screen and into the physical world, location-aware interfaces turn the player's sensory experience of real places into a storytelling tool.

In our essay, we theorize the storytelling potential unique to mobile games and describe our experience trying to use that potential when designing and building our hybrid-reality game, University of Death.

Subject: Study Results: Lung Tissue Volume and Aeration Analysis

Dear Customer,

I hope this message finds you well.

Here is what our analysis of lung tissue volume and functional changes showed.

We calculated total lung tissue volume as: volume of lung tissue = number of voxels × volume of the voxel, counting any compartment with a CT number above zero.

Next, we measured how withdrawing PEEP changed functional residual capacity (ΔFRC). That is the difference in total gas volume in the whole lung between PEEP and ZEEP. Alveolar derecruitment we defined as the difference in gas volume within poorly aerated and nonaerated regions between those same two states.

For normally aerated regions, where CT attenuation sits between -500 and -900 HU, we tracked the gas volume lost when PEEP came off (see Figure 2).

Finally, following reference [21], we classified each patient's distribution of lost aeration (lung morphology) as diffuse, patchy, or lobar, based on CT attenuation distribution at ZEEP.

This package brings together datasets, constants, conversion factors, and utilities for Marine, Riverine, Estuarine, LAcustrine, and Coastal science. It supplies (1) chemical and physical constants and datasets like atomic weights, gas constants, and Earth bathymetry.
